PMGT1711 Week 08

PMGT1711 Week 8 - Relational Complexity and Social Network Analysis

Projects within Social Systems

A project is both a system in its own right and part of wider social, political, economic and environmental systems. Its difficulties can change over time: work that initially appears straightforward may become complicated through numerous dependencies or complex through adaptation, conflict and unpredictable interactions.

Relational complexity concerns how intertwined human relationships and power dynamics affect outcomes. Alliances, conflict, trust, information sharing and exclusion can determine whether technically manageable work succeeds.

Form of complexity

Main concern

Structural

Numerous elements and interdependencies

Technical

Innovation and uncertainty about methods or design

Directional

Unclear or contested objectives

Temporal

Changing external conditions over time

Relational

Relationships, trust, conflict, power and participation

Project outcomes depend on more than the allocation of tasks. Information and influence are unevenly distributed: some groups mobilise support through networks while others remain outside important conversations. These issues are especially significant in partnerships, cross-sector work, public-private collaboration and international development.

Relevant management capabilities include stakeholder mapping, facilitation, negotiation, relationship building and trust building. A stakeholder is a person or group with an interest in, influence on, or exposure to a project's effects. Facilitation structures discussion so that participants can engage constructively.

Recognising Relational Complexity

Relational difficulties become visible through patterns such as:

• Groups that rarely communicate despite depending on each other.

• Repeated domination of discussion by the same voices.

• Uncertainty about whom to trust.

• Protection of organisational territory rather than collaboration.

• Perceptions that the project creates winners and losers.

• Selective sharing or withholding of information.

Useful analysis identifies where influence actually resides, how competing interests interact, and whose perspective is absent. Formal reporting lines alone cannot show the full social system.

Mental Models and Interacting Perspectives

A mental model is a person's underlying understanding of how a situation works. It shapes what that person sees as a problem or an acceptable response. Relational complexity emerges when different understandings interact, clash or become aligned.

A worldview is a broader interpretation of what matters and why an activity is meaningful. Soft systems tools can reveal these interpretations:

• Rich pictures: free-form visualisations of people, relationships, tensions and different perspectives.

• Root definitions: concise statements of what a purposeful system does, how, and why.

• CATWOE: an analysis of Customers, Actors, Transformation, Worldview, Owners and Environmental constraints. Customers benefit or suffer; actors carry out the transformation; owners can stop it; the worldview explains its meaning; environmental constraints are treated as given.

Network tools complement this inquiry by showing how the holders of these perspectives are connected.

Three Systems Perspectives on Relationships

Edge of Chaos

The edge of chaos describes a condition between rigid order and destructive disorder. In a project, relationships may sit between cooperation and conflict, with small changes shifting the balance.

Some disagreement can reveal hidden interests and support genuine alignment. Premature agreement may conceal distrust or unequal influence. The management task is to sustain productive discussion without allowing escalating conflict, withdrawal or loss of trust.

Stakeholder dialogues, facilitated discussions and network-building processes can help. A trusted intermediary can maintain engagement without silencing differences. Formal governance remains relevant, but cannot by itself create the quality of relationships needed.

Communication and Structure

Tense relationships can fragment communication into isolated groups, distrust and selective information sharing. Some participants dominate while others withdraw.

Structured dialogue, network visualisation and stakeholder mapping can create more legitimate communication spaces. Ground rules support respectful participation. The aim is not simply to standardise procedures, but to establish conditions in which participants can speak, be heard and build trust.

Sensitivity to Initial Conditions

Early interactions can set a durable pattern of trust or distrust. Initial exclusion or perceived unfairness may become difficult to reverse and can harden into conflict. Inclusive engagement at the beginning is therefore an investment in later cooperation.

This is sensitivity to initial conditions: small early differences can contribute to substantially different later patterns through continuing interactions. It does not mean that every small event inevitably causes a large effect.

Stakeholder Network Maps

A stakeholder network map represents people or groups as nodes and relationships as ties or edges. It depicts the human structure of a project rather than its technical work breakdown.

A sociogram is a visual representation of a social network. Colours, shapes and sizes can show attributes such as organisational affiliation, connection patterns or the duration of interactions. The meaning of every visual feature should be defined in a legend.

One qualitative notation is:

Mark

Meaning

Solid line

Alliance or cooperative relationship

Dotted line

Conflict

+ beside a node

Trusted participant

- beside a node

Distrusted participant

Larger box

Greater centrality in the depicted network

Circle around a node

Exclusion from participation

These conventions are choices for this mapping method, not universal meanings of network symbols. In particular, a dotted conflict line represents an existing relationship, not an absence of contact.

Social Network Analysis

Social Network Analysis (SNA) is a research approach for mapping and examining patterns of relationships. It can make informal work and influence visible and inform organisational or policy decisions.

Network data may come from questionnaires, interviews, observation, administrative archives or a combination. Observation can reveal interactions within a shared setting; questionnaires and interviews can capture relationships spread across organisations and places.

Network Positions and Properties

Concept

Meaning

Interpretive value

Central actor

An actor occupying a well-connected or otherwise influential position

May affect the flow of information and coordination

Peripheral actor

An actor with relatively few connections

May be less included but may introduce new information

Isolated actor

An actor with no ties in the network as defined

May lack access to the interactions being examined

Broker

An actor connecting groups that would otherwise be disconnected

Can bridge information and coordination gaps

Degree

Number of direct connections a node has

Describes immediate connectedness

Transitivity

Extent to which a person's contacts are connected to one another

Describes closure among connected groups

Centrality refers to a node's position or prominence according to a specified network property. A qualitative map may use it broadly; numerical analysis requires a clearly defined measure. Brokerage is the bridging function performed by a broker.

Two actors can have the same degree but different local structures. If one person's contacts all know one another while the other's do not, the two positions provide different access to repeated versus diverse information. Structure also affects exposure to what travels through the network, whether useful ideas or harmful influences.

Managing Relational Complexity

Project managers must balance competing interests and power differences, create space for constructive dialogue, maintain legitimacy during difficult trade-offs, and include marginalised voices. Progress may depend more on informal networks than on formal hierarchy.

Three complementary tool families support this work:

Family

Examples

Purpose

Problem structuring

Rich pictures, root definitions and CATWOE

Reveal purposes, assumptions and competing interpretations

Facilitation and engagement

Stakeholder analysis, mapping and structured dialogue

Identify interests and influence and establish conditions for participation

Network-based analysis

SNA and stakeholder network maps

Examine relationships, trust, influence and exclusion

Boundary critique examines how decisions about who and what count affect an analysis. Critical Systems Heuristics provides guiding questions for examining the assumptions and interests embedded in those boundaries, including who is included and who bears consequences without a voice.

Maps can be developed by collecting participants' accounts of trust, conflict and cooperation, then comparing them. A sudden change, such as withdrawal of government funding, can be used to examine how relationships might alter. Such a scenario is a prospective exploration, not evidence that the change actually occurred. Updating ties after changes shows that relational complexity is dynamic.

Cases

Wind Farm Development

A large wind farm may have manageable turbine design, grid connection and construction arrangements while facing difficult social relationships:

• Local farmers are concerned about land use and noise.

• Environmental non-governmental organisations seek biodiversity protection that conflicts with industry schedules.

• The energy company seeks profitability and has disproportionate influence.

• Indigenous groups seek meaningful consultation about cultural heritage sites.

• A divided local council struggles to establish a common position.

Here, fractured relationships, unequal influence and competing interests can undermine progress despite a workable technical design. A non-governmental organisation (NGO) is an organisation outside government; the environmental groups in this scenario advocate environmental interests.

A Five-Person Team

Maya coordinates a team involving Sam, Lily, Raj and Tom. Cooperative ties connect Maya with Sam, Lily and Raj, and Lily with Raj. Sam and Tom have fallen out. Tom has become quiet and excluded.

       [Lily] -------- [Raj]
           \          /
            [MAYA +]
              /
           [Sam] . . . . ((Tom -))

Solid connection: cooperation
Dotted connection: conflict
Maya: central and trusted
Double parentheses: excluded participant
Minus sign: low trust in the depicted situation

Coordination is concentrated through Maya. Her departure would therefore threaten continuity. Tom's exclusion also threatens completion of his contribution. The technical work can remain feasible while the social configuration creates delivery risk.

Marine Park Rollout

A state government proposes a coastal marine park to protect biodiversity and encourage tourism.

Stakeholder

Interests and position

State government

Growth, tourism and favourable public attention

Tourism board

More visitors and alignment with government promotion

Fishers' association

Protection of livelihoods threatened by fishing restrictions

Environmental NGO

Strong conservation measures and strict limits

Indigenous custodians council

Meaningful authority and participation concerning its Country, despite a history of exclusion

Marine scientists

Decisions informed by evidence rather than political pressure

National media organisation

Coverage that may amplify conflict or build support

Government and tourism interests align in this scenario. Fishers and the environmental organisation disagree over restrictions. These given relationships do not establish every participant's ties; a complete map would require further inquiry rather than assumed alliances.

Campus Redevelopment

A university plans new teaching spaces, a student centre and expanded accommodation.

Stakeholder

Interests and position

University executive

Reputation, donor satisfaction and timely delivery

Alumni donors network

Prestigious facilities and naming recognition

Student union

Affordable spaces and meaningful rather than symbolic influence

Local council

Planning approval, traffic, noise and community effects

Contractors and developers

Cost and schedule control, with resistance to expensive additions

Campus sustainability group

Ambitious environmental standards

Local business association

More customers without disruptive construction effects

The executive and donor network align around prestige. Contractors and the sustainability group face tension between cost control and environmental ambition. A network map helps examine which interests can coordinate and which voices are omitted.

Influence, Contagion and Emergence

Social influence can extend beyond direct contacts. A person may be affected by changes transmitted through a contact's other relationships. The widower effect describes an association between losing a spouse and elevated mortality risk for the surviving partner; it motivates inquiry into health effects arising through relationships.

Network studies have examined clustering in body weight, smoking, drinking, voting, divorce, altruism and emotions. Clustering means similar characteristics appear together in connected parts of a network. At least three explanations must be considered:

Explanation

Meaning

Induction or social influence

People influence one another's behaviour, norms or states

Homophily

Similar people preferentially form relationships

Confounding

Shared conditions influence connected people, creating an apparent relationship between their characteristics

An association among connected people does not, by itself, distinguish these mechanisms. Claims that influence reliably extends exactly three relationship steps should not be treated as a universal law.

Emotional contagion describes the spread of emotional expression or responses through social interaction. Behavioural imitation and changing norms can also transmit influence. A multicentric process has multiple centres rather than a single starting individual.

Networks change as people enter or leave and ties form or break. They can retain patterns beyond individual members. Happiness and unhappiness may cluster, and network position can affect exposure to support, information or distress; clustering alone still does not establish causation.

Social capital is the value accessible through social relationships and their structure. The contrast between graphite and diamond offers an analogy: the same basic units can have different properties because they are connected differently. Likewise, collective capability depends on ties as well as individual qualities.

A superorganism is a collective interpreted as having coordinated properties that exceed those of isolated members. Examples such as coordinated animal groups illustrate emergence: group-level patterns arise from interaction. Human networks can similarly affect innovation, bank runs and collective action. A complex adaptive system is a system whose interacting participants adapt, generating changing collective patterns.

Networks carry both benefits and harms, including ideas, kindness, misinformation, violence and disease. For projects, the practical implication is to examine both the architecture of relationships and what moves through it, including trust, distrust, knowledge and influence.
